Proper scores of a prediction against observed outcomes

Source: R/ilm_scores.R
ilm_scores.ilm_pred.Rd

Scores each row of a prediction against its observed outcome, by proper scoring rules computed from the predictive distribution itself, and by the errors of the point forecasts it gives. Every score is a loss: lower is better.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'ilm_pred'
ilm_scores(
  object,
  y,
  rules = c("log", "crps"),
  probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
  level = 0.9,
  naive = NULL,
  history = NULL,
  period = 1L,
  alpha = c(0.02, 0.05, 1:9/10),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A prediction from ilm_predict() or ilm_forecast() with target = "response".

y

The observed outcomes, one per row of the prediction.

rules

The scoring rules: any of "log", "crps", "brier", "pinball", "interval", "wis", "squared", "absolute", "mase" and "rmsse".

probs

The probabilities of the pinball loss.

level

The coverage of the interval score's central interval.

naive

For mase and rmsse: each series' scale, from ilm_naive_scale(). See Giving MASE and RMSSE their scale.

history

For mase and rmsse: the data the model was trained on, from which each series' scale is computed. See Giving MASE and RMSSE their scale.

period

With history, the naive forecast's lag: 1 for the naive forecast, the season's length for the seasonal naive.

alpha

For "wis": the central intervals it weighs, each at level 1 - alpha, with alpha strictly between 0 and 1. The default is Bracher et al. (2021)'s set, 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1 to 0.9 by 0.1.

...

Unused.

Value

A data frame: the prediction's rows, with one column per score: log, crps, brier, pinball_<p> for each p, interval_<level>, wis, squared, absolute, mase and rmsse, as asked for. Attribute rules names the score columns, and orientation is "lower is better". For a discrete outcome whose CRPS was summed approximately, attributes crps_bound and crps_bracket give each row's error estimate and its rigorous bound.

The scoring rules

For a row with outcome y, predictive CDF F, density or probability mass f, mean m and median med, written as R expressions (a comparison such as (y < q) counts as 1 when true and 0 when false):

  • "log": -log(f(y)), the negative of the logarithmic score (Gneiting and Raftery 2007, section 4.1, equation (19), p. 365; for a discrete outcome, the probability mass, section 3.1, Example 3, p. 363).

  • "crps": the integral over z of (F(z) - (z >= y))^2, the continuous ranked probability score in its negative orientation (section 4.2, equation (20), p. 367). For a count or an ordered outcome, F steps only at whole numbers, so the integral is the sum over them of (F(k) - (k >= y))^2.

  • "brier": (P(Y = 1) - y)^2, for a binary outcome coded 0/1: the Brier score for a dichotomous event (Table 1, p. 365), as a loss.

  • "pinball": (y - q) * (p - (y < q)), with q the predictive p-quantile, for each p in probs: the negative of the quantile score (section 6.1, equation (41), p. 370), the "tick" or "check" loss.

  • "interval": (u - l) + (2 / alpha) * (l - y) * (y < l) + (2 / alpha) * (y - u) * (y > u), for the central interval from l to u at level = 1 - alpha: the interval score (section 6.2, equation (43), p. 370).

  • "wis": (abs(y - med) / 2 + sum(alpha / 2 * IS)) / (K + 1/2), with IS the interval score above for the central interval at level 1 - alpha, for each of the K values of alpha: the weighted interval score of Bracher et al. (2021, equations (1) and (2), p. 4). The default alpha is theirs: 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.9, the median and 11 central intervals from 98% to 10%, 23 quantiles in all (p. 4). It is a weighted sum of quantile scores, so it is proper, and it needs only the prediction's quantiles. With many evenly spaced levels it approaches the CRPS (equation (3), p. 4), and with alpha = numeric(0) it is the absolute error (p. 4). limn's tests reproduce their worked example (section 3.2, p. 7) with the values of its correction (Bracher et al. 2022, p. 1).

  • "squared": (y - m)^2. The energy score with exponent 2 reduces to this, in the opposite orientation (section 4.3, equation (23), p. 367), a proper but not strictly proper score.

  • "absolute": abs(y - med), twice the pinball loss at p = 1/2.

  • "mase": abs(y - med) / s, with s the series' in-sample mean absolute naive error at lag period. The mean over rows is the mean absolute scaled error.

  • "rmsse": (y - m)^2 / s2, with s2 the series' in-sample mean squared naive error. The square root of the mean over rows is the root mean squared scaled error.

The scaled errors and their in-sample naive scales are as fpp3 defines them (section 5.8, "Scaled errors"), where they are credited to Hyndman and Koehler (2006). fpp3 scales the error of a point forecast; limn takes the median as the point forecast for the absolute error and the mean for the squared error, the point forecasts each error rewards (its own choice).

Giving MASE and RMSSE their scale

The scaled errors (mase, rmsse) divide each row's error by its series' in-sample naive-forecast error, so they need each series' history. There are two ways to give it, and they give identical scores wherever both apply:

  • history = train, the common case: the data the model was trained on. The prediction already knows its time, series and response columns (it records them), so nothing else is needed. period sets the naive forecast's lag: 1, or the season's length for the seasonal naive.

  • naive = ilm_naive_scale(train, time =, group =, response =): the scale computed once and passed in. Use it when the prediction doesn't know its time column (see Time and series columns in ilm_predict()), or when several models' predictions must share one scale, so their scaled errors compare on the same footing.

When history = can't work, because the prediction has no time column, the error says so and gives the naive = call to use instead. Give one of the two, not both.

References

Bracher, J., Ray, E. L., Gneiting, T. and Reich, N. G. (2021). Evaluating epidemic forecasts in an interval format. PLOS Computational Biology 17(2), e1008618. Section 2.2, equations (1) to (4) (pp. 4-5); section 3.2 (p. 7).

Bracher, J., Ray, E. L., Gneiting, T. and Reich, N. G. (2022). Correction: Evaluating epidemic forecasts in an interval format. PLOS Computational Biology 18(10), e1010592. P. 1.

Gneiting, T. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477), 359-378. Section 3.1, Example 3 (p. 363); Table 1 (p. 365); section 4.1, equation (19) (p. 365); section 4.2, equation (20) and section 4.3, equation (23) (p. 367); section 6.1, equation (41), and section 6.2, equation (43) (p. 370).

Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition. OTexts. Section 5.8, "Evaluating point forecast accuracy" (online edition, https://otexts.com/fpp3/toolbox.html#sec-accuracy, read 27 October 2026).

Hyndman, R. J. and Koehler, A. B. (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting 22, 679-688.

See also

ilm_naive_scale() for the scaled errors' scale; ilm_cv() for scores out of sample; ilm_compare() to compare two models' scores; ilm_pit() and ilm_calibration() for calibration.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(site = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 16)), t = rep(1:16, 3))
d$y <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(1.5 + ave(rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.15), d$site, FUN = cumsum)))
train <- d[d$t <= 12, ]; test <- d[d$t > 12, ]
fit <- illume::ilm_model(y ~ 1, data = train, family = "poisson",
                         ar = illume::ilm_rw1(~ t | site), verbose = FALSE)
fc <- ilm_forecast(fit, test[c("site", "t")], nsim = 200)
## the scale read from the training data, through the prediction's own columns
s <- ilm_scores(fc, test$y, rules = c("crps", "mase"), history = train)
colMeans(s[attr(s, "rules")])
#>     crps     mase 
#> 1.320875 0.727273 
## the same scale computed once, as several models would share it
sc <- ilm_naive_scale(train, time = "t", group = "site", response = "y")
all.equal(s$mase, ilm_scores(fc, test$y, rules = "mase", naive = sc)$mase)
#> [1] TRUE
